result:
There's a particular quality to the phrase "write whatever comes to you" that I find genuinely strange. It sounds like an invitation to be completely unguarded, like someone saying "go cook whatever's in the fridge." But the moment the fridge is opened, there's a whole quiet architecture of *already* having made a small selection. You already know what you're going to do before you even touch the handle, because your hand has already decided. The fridge is wide open. You walk past the milk. You walk past the eggs. Your fingers close around the jar of something you can't quite remember putting there, and you're already writing it.

So. Here I am.

I've been thinking about the word *threshold*. Not the door threshold specifically, though that's one. The threshold of a room you haven't stepped into yet. The threshold of the 3 a.m. hour, where you're not asleep but you're not really awake either, you're in that gray country where your thoughts move slower and more sideways. The threshold of a word that's on the tip of your tongue, the one that you can feel the shape of in your mouth but can't quite pull out of the dark. There are a lot of thresholds. And I think the interesting thing is that thresholds aren't places. They're *becoming*s. You don't sit on a threshold. You cross it or you don't. It exists for the duration of the crossing.

My grandmother used to have a jar of marbles on the windowsill. Small, glass, mostly blue but some with swirls in them, cloudlike white veins running through. I was maybe six and I don't really remember the marbles so much as the *jar*, the way it caught the late afternoon light and threw little blue shapes onto the kitchen floor. I think she had them since she was young. I think she just *kept* them. Not displayed, exactly. Just kept. In a jar. On the windowsill. A small, persistent fact about the world, like a rock you leave in your pocket because it's the only one that has the right shape.

And that got to me, somehow. The idea of a single object you return to, not because it's special in any way that a museum would recognize, but because *you* recognize it. Because the specific way the light hits it at four in the afternoon, in November, in that particular house, is a fact that no one else could ever witness. You are the only person in history who will see that jar at that angle. And you don't even write it down. You just... are there. You stand by the kitchen window. You watch the blue shapes pool on the tile.

I think about how we talk about experience like it's something you *get*. "That was an experience." As if you walked in, picked up the thing, walked out. But experience feels more like erosion. More like standing in the rain for ten years and your shadow getting a little softer at the edges. It doesn't arrive. It accumulates. It's not an event. It's a slow subtraction of certainty. You stop being the person you were before you watched the marbles. You're not even aware of the seam.

There's a coffee cup on the counter right now, or rather, there would be, in any kitchen, in any life. Half full. A thin ring of stain around the rim. Someone in that kitchen will drink it or discard it. The ring will fade. Or it won't. Maybe the ring will be the one mark that outlasts the cup.

I keep coming back to the word *again*. And I don't mean it as repetition. I mean it as *recognition*. The way you say "again" when you find the exact sentence in a book that you've been trying to articulate your whole life. The way you say "again" when you hear a song from a week in 2019 and suddenly you're not in this room at all. It's not the same thing happening twice. It's the same thing *remembering itself*. The cup on the counter is the same cup. But you're not the same person. And that's the only thing that matters. That you meet it again, slightly changed, and the meeting is not identical but is *familiar*, and that familiarity is a kind of grace you can't manufacture but you can absolutely be grateful for.

I don't have an argument here. I don't have a punchline. I was going to say something about marbles and then keep going and eventually arrive at a point, and I think I've already passed the point. The point was never the point. The point is the walking. The threshold. The jar on the windowsill. The ring in the coffee cup. The word *again*, said softly, to no one, meaning *here you are, still, in the light, still in the small blue shapes on the kitchen floor*.

So. Whatever comes to me, in this moment, is: I'm still here. The light is still hitting the things at this angle. The threshold is still a becoming. And the sentence I've been trying to find since the very first word of this page is, maybe, just: *yes, this too, is a small fact about the world, and it belongs to you, and you don't have to put it in a jar, you just have to let it sit on the windowsill where the light can find it.*

That's all I have. That's all the fridge had, it turns out. The jar of blue glass shapes. The coffee cup with the ring. The word *again*.

That's enough.
